source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events (abstract via colab.ws)
finding: Founding paper. Two experiments on explaining events set in the future or the past, and sure or uncertain. Exp 1: temporal perspective had little effect; outcome certainty shaped explanations. Exp 2: uncertainty changes which kind of explanation people pick, not how long they spend.
numbers: Sure-event explanations were longer, had a higher share of episodic reasons, and were in past tense. No statistics on the abstract page.
quote: Explanations for sure events tended to be longer, to contain a higher proportion of episodic reasons
limits: Only the abstract was read, not the full text. The paper did not test a premortem or any plan. J Behav Decis Making 2(1), 25-38.
agent_relevance: The key is certainty of outcome (treat failure as fixed), not time travel. Use a failure frame only as a probe, with the cause list checked by code.

source: Review page on premortem evidence (corporate.jcx.au/premortem), summarising Mitchell 1989
finding: Secondary summary: Mitchell et al. found that imagining the event as certain gave about 30% more reasons for a future outcome. It says reason quality was not assessed, and that Klein 2007 overstated this as better ability to identify correct reasons.
numbers: About 30% more reasons. Exact N and test not given.
limits: Secondary source. The 30% is not on the abstract I read. Unverified against the primary paper.
agent_relevance: Count of reasons is not accuracy of reasons. Score generated failure causes by whether a check confirms them, not by number.

source: Same review page: Veinott, Klein, Wiggins (2010) PreMortem and plan confidence
finding: 178 university students judged an H1N1 lockdown plan across five conditions. Imagining the plan had failed cut confidence more than other methods, about twice the drop of Pros/Cons or Cons-only.
numbers: N=178; 5 conditions; about 2x the confidence drop of pros/cons and cons-only. No test statistics given.
limits: Students, hypothetical scenario, outcome is confidence not plan quality. Reviewer calls the base thin. No replication stated.
agent_relevance: Premortem lowers confidence, which is the impasse trigger we want, but a confidence drop does not prove better plans.

source: Same review page: Gallop and Bischoff (2016) How to catch a black swan
finding: 101 experienced program managers and engineers in teams of 4-6 compared premortem with traditional brainstorming on a torpedo proximity-fuse scenario in 45 minutes. A blind panel scored risks and plan changes. Premortem teams found more quality risks, had more effective plan changes, and found more black swan risks.
numbers: N=101; quality = panel score above 70 on both creativity and plausibility/usefulness. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: No effect sizes or p-values on the page. One scenario, short task, no replication stated. J Enterprise Transformation 6(2), 87-106.
agent_relevance: Best outcome-style evidence for premortem as a risk finder, but only versus brainstorming and only in groups.

source: Klein (2007) Performing a project premortem, HBR 85(9) (summary page)
finding: Practitioner article that introduced the premortem: the team assumes the project has just failed, then writes plausible reasons. Aim: make it safe for knowledgeable dissenters to speak.
numbers: No numbers on the open page; the 30% claim and the Mitchell citation are not on the visible summary.
quote: In a premortem, team members assume that the project they are planning has just failed
limits: Only summary and intro were visible. Business examples are anecdotes, not evidence.
agent_relevance: The procedure is the template for an impasse-triggered failure probe.

source: Klein (2021) The pre-mortem method, Psychology Today
finding: Procedure: brief the team, say the plan has failed as if a crystal ball showed it, 2 minutes silent writing, round-robin one item each with the leader first. Later additions: 2 minutes for actions against the problems, and rating each problem for likelihood, impact and ease of prevention.
numbers: Session 20-30 minutes; 2 minutes writing; Veinott 2010 cited with 178 students.
limits: Author invented the technique. Benefits (candor, trust, mental models) have no numbers there. Named mistake: asking what could go wrong instead of asserting failure.
agent_relevance: The rating step maps to code ranking of candidate failure causes. Assert failure, do not ask.

source: Wikipedia: Pre-mortem
finding: Cites Klein 2007 and Kahneman 2011, and names Mitchell et al. 1989 for prospective hindsight, with no outcome evidence or numbers.
numbers: None.
limits: Confirms the task note that the page cites no outcome evidence.
agent_relevance: The evidence base is thin; do not assume premortem works for an LLM without testing.

source: Gary Klein site, premortem page
finding: Short description: leader briefs the plan, asks the team to imagine it has failed, everyone lists threats. No evidence cited.
numbers: None.
limits: Practitioner page.
agent_relevance: Procedure only.

source: Wikipedia: Hindsight bias
finding: Background: Fischhoff 1975 gave a story with four outcomes, told people one was true, and they rated the told outcome as more likely. Debiasing mostly fails, except by considering how alternatives could be true.
numbers: No figures on the page.
limits: Only the first 100000 characters were read. The premortem uses the same certainty effect that causes hindsight bias, but for good.
agent_relevance: Supports firing a counterfactual probe on a signal; awareness of bias alone does not fix it.

source: Veinott, Klein, Wiggins (2010) Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence, ISCRAM (full text via web.archive.org copy)
finding: The only controlled test of the premortem as Klein defined it. Students read a flawed H1N1 campus lockdown plan, rated confidence 0-100, then did one of five tasks for about two minutes (filler baseline, critique, pro/cons, cons only, premortem). Premortem cut confidence most.
numbers: N=178 students (62% female, mean age 19), groups of 5-6. Time-1 confidence did not differ (F(4,173)=1.44). Change in confidence Time1 to Time2: premortem M=-25.0 points, pro-con -14.0, cons-only -12.4, critique and baseline about 0. Condition effect F(5,173)=30.88, p<.0001. Premortem vs pro-con t(74)=-7.08; vs cons-only t(67)=-8.42. Pilot confidence for the plan was 67%.
quote: Premortem group: assume the plan failed, then explain why.
limits: Student sample, ready-made plan, no responsibility to implement, one scenario, outcome is stated confidence not plan quality or real failure rate. Authors flag that all arms wrote individually first, which inflates rivals.
agent_relevance: Shows failure-framing lowers stated confidence about twice as much as just listing cons. For our agent a drop in self-rated confidence is only a trigger; the check that the listed causes are real must be done by code or tools.

source: Veinott et al. (2010), same paper: improvement phase and understanding
finding: After the failure list, each person spent two more minutes proposing fixes. Premortem confidence recovered most, but it started lowest. Subjective understanding of the plan rose for premortem, pro-con and cons-only relative to baseline, but not relative to critique.
numbers: Time2 to Time3 condition effect F(5,173)=72.54 (as printed), p<.0001; premortem beat pro-con t(74)=-4.42. Understanding: omnibus F(5,173)=1.92 n.s.; premortem t(74)=1.97, pro-con t(67)=2.02, cons-only t(54)=1.88, each p<.05 vs baseline only.
limits: Recovery may simply be regression from the lowest point; the authors say so. Quality of the failure reasons and of the fixes was not scored in this paper. Degrees of freedom and F are printed oddly (5 df for five conditions).
agent_relevance: The useful part is the second step: failure causes then fixes. Build the loop as list causes, rank, then repair, and measure plan quality afterwards, not confidence.

source: Veinott et al. (2010), same paper: stated mechanisms and theory
finding: Authors propose two mechanisms: focus on failure, and a certain (not probabilistic) outcome. They cite Mitchell 1989 as raising explanation count by about 30%, Koriat 1980 on one-sided reasons, and the data/frame model: the premortem forces a figure-ground reversal so anomalies get taken seriously. They also cite Nemeth 2001 that devil's advocates are ineffective because criticism looks inauthentic.
numbers: Pro-con and cons-only each gave about half the premortem drop, read by the authors as both mechanisms contributing. The 30% figure is quoted second-hand, not re-measured.
limits: Mechanism is inferred from the pattern of means, not tested by manipulating certainty and failure focus separately. The paper gives no premortem-specific data on reason counts.
agent_relevance: Design rule: do not play devil's advocate against your own plan. State the failure as a fact in the prompt, then explain. Keep that frame in the scaffold as an impasse trigger.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future, J Behav Decis Making 2(1):25-38 (Crossref abstract and reference list, Semantic Scholar record)
finding: Abstract defines prospective hindsight: explain a future event as if it had happened. Two experiments crossed temporal perspective (future vs past) with outcome uncertainty (certain vs uncertain). Perspective had little effect; certainty strongly changed the explanations: longer, more episodic reasons, past tense. Exp 2: uncertainty changes the type of explanation, not time spent.
numbers: Crossref lists 22 references and 91 citing works; Semantic Scholar shows 108. References include Fischhoff 1980, Hogarth 1983 (imagination as experience), Holland 1986, Abelson 1976, Weick 1979, Ward, Hastie and Taylor 1978. Cell sizes and test statistics are not in the abstract and the paper itself is paywalled.
quote: Explanations for sure events tended to be longer, to contain a higher proportion of episodic reasons
limits: Full text not opened; the oft-quoted '30% more reasons' appears only in Veinott 2010 and web summaries, not in the abstract. Study explained events, never evaluated a plan.
agent_relevance: The proven lever is certainty of the outcome. Ask the agent to explain a fixed failure, and compare the count and type of causes against an uncertain-framing control.

source: Peabody (2017) Improving planning: quantitative evaluation of the premortem in field and laboratory settings, Michigan Tech PhD thesis (abstract page)
finding: Three experiments. Army cadets in field exercises: premortem teams made fewer mistakes and showed less fixation, with no change in planning or execution time. University students: premortem vs worst-case scenario gave similar counts of reasons but different categories. Exp 3: premortem gave more reasons than worst case; groups gave more solutions than individuals.
numbers: No sample sizes or statistics on the abstract page; the PDF returned HTTP 403.
limits: Abstract only. Not peer reviewed. Worst-case is a close rival method, so the gain over it is small or about content type.
agent_relevance: One of very few outcome-flavoured tests (fewer mistakes). Supports using a premortem pass before action, and comparing it to a worst-case pass in our own ablations.

source: Blank, Musch, Pohl (2007) Hindsight bias: on being wise after the event, Social Cognition 25(1):1-9 (Fischhoff 1975 as described)
finding: Describes Fischhoff (1975). Exp 1: historical, political and clinical case scenarios; people given the outcome judged it more probable than people judging in foresight. Exp 2: instruction to ignore the outcome did not remove it. Exp 3: judging as another uninformed person did not remove it. Named creeping determinism; judges did not notice the shift.
numbers: Review counts over 150 articles and two meta-analyses since 1975. Cell sizes and means from the 1975 paper not given here (PDF copies tried returned HTML).
limits: Second-hand account of the founding paper. Primary numbers not recovered this session.
agent_relevance: Hindsight is why a premortem is needed: an agent that sees a failure will make it look inevitable. Instruction alone does not fix it, so the scaffold must change the task, not just ask for neutrality.

source: Blank, Musch, Pohl (2007), same overview: manifestations and explanation models
finding: Two main forms: distorted outcome probability and distorted memory for earlier judgments (Fischhoff and Beyth 1975 on Nixon visits; Fischhoff 1977 Aladdin). Explanation families: immediate assimilation, reconstruction, computational models SARA and RAFT, causal sense-making models, surprise, and metacognitive fluency. No single theory covers all.
numbers: Models named: SARA (Pohl 2003), RAFT (Hoffrage 2000), multinomial model (Erdfelder and Buchner 1998), causal model (Pezzo 2003; Hawkins and Hastie 1990).
limits: Overview, not new data. The premortem is not itself a hindsight-bias debiaser; it borrows the same sense-making machinery.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal models the field uses. For an agent the causal sense-making account matters: once told an outcome, the model builds a coherent chain and feels sure about it.

source: Blank, Musch, Pohl (2007), same overview: debiasing and learning
finding: Warnings reduce bias little; counterfactual instructions sometimes help but usually only with great effort. Hindsight may block learning from experience, yet some authors treat it as a by-product of adaptive learning. Little research tests the link to learning.
numbers: Cited: Pohl and Hell 1996, Wood 1978, Hasher et al 1981 (trivia only), Hawkins and Hastie 1990.
limits: Overview.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'be unbiased' prompts. Use structural moves: force alternative outcomes with their own causes.

source: Guilbault et al. (2004) hindsight bias meta-analysis; Christensen-Szalanski and Willham (1991) (via search snippets only)
finding: Snippets report Guilbault: 95 studies, 252 effect sizes, mean d=0.39 (95% CI .36 to .42), debiasing manipulations had no significant effect. Christensen-Szalanski: 122 or 128 studies, small overall effect (r=.17 on one listing), larger when task is familiar.
numbers: d=0.39; r=.17; familiarity moderator r=.42 (secondary).
limits: Not opened; counts and figures conflict between listings. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Size of the problem a premortem fights is moderate; formal debiasing is known to work poorly, which is why a method with a task change is worth testing.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for confidence, JEP: Human Learning and Memory 6(2):107-118, Experiment 1
finding: Core precursor. Subjects answered two-alternative general knowledge questions and gave probability correct. In the reasons condition they first wrote reasons for and against each alternative. Calibration improved markedly; some overconfidence stayed at 0.9 and 1.0.
numbers: 73 paid volunteers, 5 dropped, 68 analysed; each answered two of six 15-question sets (first 5 items warm-up), control then reasons; 9-13 per set (control) and 10-12 (reasons). Effects tested by jackknife over 68 samples; exact table values not recovered from PDF text. Control showed typical overconfidence.
limits: Within-subject, control always first (order checks on other sets found no effect). Trivia items only. Reasons were written before choosing.
agent_relevance: The ancestor of 'think about why you might be wrong'. Our premortem is the one-sided, certainty version of it.

source: Koriat et al. (1980), Experiment 2 and follow-up
finding: After choosing, subjects listed one supporting reason, one contradicting reason, or both. Only contradicting reasons improved calibration; supporting reasons had no effect. Subjects found one contradicting reason hardest to produce. Correlations suggest confidence follows the amount and strength of evidence for the chosen answer.
numbers: 200 paid volunteers, 66 per group; 11 removed from the contradicting group for writing supporting reasons. Follow-up 44 subjects. Subjects wrote on average 18.3 reasons for vs 13.4 against in Exp 1, t(61)=7.99. Contradicting effect smaller than full reasons condition of Exp 1.
limits: Fischhoff and Macgregor (1982) reportedly failed to replicate the effect (see a22). Calibration changed through lower confidence plus slight rise in accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supports forcing a counter-case after an answer is chosen. Predicts agents will drift back to supporting reasons unless the failure frame is imposed.

source: Arkes, Faust, Guilmette, Hart (1988) Eliminating the hindsight bias, J Applied Psychology 73(2):305-307
finding: Mailed survey of neuropsychologists using one case history and three diagnoses. Hindsight groups told one diagnosis was correct. Groups also asked to write a reason each diagnosis might be correct showed less bias. Closest early test of a 'reasons for other outcomes' debias in experts.
numbers: 480 mailed, 194 returned (40%), 8 cells of 22-30. Biased in hindsight: 42 of 72 (58%) vs 28 of 68 (41%) with reasons; chi2(1,N=140)=4.12, p<.05. Warnings tried by Fischhoff 1977 and Wood 1978 had failed.
limits: Single case, low return rate, bias measured as share above foresight mean, ipsative probabilities.
agent_relevance: Best single evidence that writing reasons for the non-observed outcomes helps experts. Argues for 'explain each alternative outcome' as an agent move.

source: Arkes et al. (1988), citing Lord, Lepper, Preston (1984) and Fischhoff and Macgregor (1982)
finding: States that Fischhoff and Macgregor (1982) could not replicate the Koriat 1980 result in a similar setting. Lord et al. 1984 'consider the opposite' reduced attitude polarization in a death-penalty study.
numbers: No numbers given for the failed replication in this note.
limits: Failed replication is reported second-hand; primary 1982 report not opened.
agent_relevance: Counter-case prompting is not a sure thing. Plan to measure it per task type.

source: Sanna and Schwarz (2004) Integrating temporal biases, Psychological Science 15(7):474-481
finding: Students listed 3 or 12 success or failure thoughts before a real exam or just after grades. Content alone did not predict the biases. Listing 3 failure thoughts (easy) pushed judgments the failure way, but 12 failure thoughts (hard) acted like success thoughts. This reproduces the premortem logic and shows how it can reverse.
numbers: N=227 introductory psychology students. Thoughts listed: 12-condition M=9.9 vs 3.0 (F(1,169)=21.33). Difficulty rated higher for 12 (M=9.1). Planned contrasts, planning fallacy t(207)=8.38; hindsight t(207)=4.83. Control students did not list thoughts.
limits: One exam context, student sample; exact condition means are not recoverable from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: asking for many failure reasons can backfire when generation feels hard. Cap the list at easy size, or have code count real items instead of using felt difficulty.

source: Schwarz, Sanna, Skurnik, Yoon (2007) Metacognitive experiences and the intricacies of setting people straight, Adv Exp Soc Psych 39:127-161
finding: Review: 'consider the opposite' and similar debiasing strategies work only when generating alternatives feels easy and backfire when it feels difficult. Misattribution of the difficulty (background music) flips the pattern; yoked readers who only read the thoughts show the normal more-is-better pattern; facial feedback (corrugator contraction) can create the effect.
numbers: Cites Schwarz 1991 assertiveness recall (6 vs 12 examples) and Sanna, Schwarz, Stocker 2002 hindsight debiasing backfire.
limits: Review of a program of social-psychology studies; effect depends on naive theories about what difficulty means.
agent_relevance: Explains the risk in prompting an LLM for long failure lists. A model has no felt effort, so the risk may be absent, but the quality of items 10-12 should be checked.

source: Sieck, Merkle, Van Zandt (2007) Option fixation: a cognitive contributor to overconfidence, OBHDP 103:68-83
finding: ASC model: people judge familiarity, then use the favoured option as a retrieval cue to build an explanation of why it is true, causing overconfidence. Exp 2 added an 'explain, independent' condition: assume each option true and explain why. This cut overconfidence further than independent rating alone, drifting to underconfidence for hard foils.
numbers: Exp 1 used a 30-item financial quiz, F(1,180) tests; Exp 2 N=141 undergraduates. Foil-plausibility effect size on confidence d=0.031 (standard), 0.126 (independent), 0.404 (explain, independent). Bias effect of elicitation method F(2,138)=9.447.
limits: Finance quiz with students; effects directional, perfect calibration not reached.
agent_relevance: A lab form of prospective hindsight: explain each option as if known true. Supports 'assume it is true, then explain' for every candidate answer, not just failures.

source: Sieck et al. (2007), same: why reasons-listing can fail
finding: Authors argue listing reasons for and against needs retrieval cues that disrupt memory search, and retrieving reasons against the favourite is especially hard, which can raise confidence (citing Sanna 2002; Yates 1992). Confirmation-bias accounts instead predict improvement. Independent evaluation of each option avoids the problem.
numbers: No new numbers beyond a25.
limits: Competing explanation for Koriat results and the Fischhoff-Macgregor failure.
agent_relevance: Gives a rival to the 'failure focus' story: independence of evaluation matters. Test premortem against independent per-option explanation.

source: Kim et al. (2025-2026) InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models, arXiv 2510.01569v3
finding: Prompting and training method: list harms, analyse consequences, then answer under constraints. Calls itself premortem reasoning, but it enumerates harms before answering; it does not assume a failure happened. Trained with SFT and GRPO on three LLM families.
numbers: Up to 32% less harmfulness vs zero-shot, 16% vs a safety prompt; TRIDENT harmfulness 3.22 to 2.19 (32.0%); SafetyBench gain about 5-13%, Illegal Activities +15.8% (N=1,767); blackmail rates cut 90%, murder attempts 44% in agentic scenarios; reasoning gains up to +5.0% GPQA, MATH500 (single seed). Frontier Claude, GPT models sat at 70-75% regardless of method.
limits: Judged by LLM ensemble; single-seed reasoning evaluation; not a test of Klein's certainty frame; no baseline that merely asks for risks without a failure assumption.
agent_relevance: Evidence that enumerating failure modes first helps safety tasks in LLMs. Does not prove the certainty frame is the active ingredient.

source: Bench to the Future 2 (2026) Evaluating strategic reasoning in forecasting agents, arXiv 2604.26106 (abstract)
finding: Pastcasting benchmark with 1,417 questions and a frozen 15M-document corpus. A built forecaster was 0.011 Brier more accurate than any single frontier agent; authors say it differed mainly in pre-mortem analysis of blind spots and consideration of black swans.
numbers: 1,417 questions; benchmark detects 0.004 Brier differences; 0.011 Brier gain.
limits: Abstract only; the pre-mortem is one of several components, so attribution is by the authors' reading of traces.
agent_relevance: Rare LLM result where a pre-mortem step is tied to forecast accuracy. Check the paper's ablation before relying on it.

source: Scott et al. (2025) What does success look like? AI-assisted prospective reflection for meetings, arXiv 2505.14370
finding: Technology probe study with a generative-AI Meeting Purpose Assistant prompting prospective reflection. Cites premortem as prior art and claims premortems improve collaborative outcomes (citing Veinott 2010 and others). Not itself a premortem test.
numbers: 18 participants used the probe; follow-up survey after meetings.
limits: Small, qualitative, premortem only cited in related work.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence; useful as a pointer that LLM assistants have been used to run prospective reflection with people.

source: Name clash: Prospective Hindsight: self-calibrating RL via prediction-reality gaps, arXiv 2610.02740
finding: Uses the words 'prospective hindsight' for a training signal: the gap between the agent's prediction before feedback and its evaluation after. Not Mitchell's explain-a-certain-failure method.
numbers: No premortem numbers; claims better task performance and calibration under GRPO and distillation (abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Same name, different idea; do not cite as evidence for the premortem.
agent_relevance: Avoid confusing it. The surprise-gap idea is a possible separate calibration signal for training, outside our no-training scope.

source: Meuer, Nestler, Oeberst (2022) What determines hindsight bias in written work? JEP: Applied
finding: Hindsight bias enters written event accounts (Wikipedia). It grows with the need to make sense of the event and with availability of causal information; content policies did not help. Consistent with causal model theory.
numbers: One field study of 40 real Wikipedia articles plus three preregistered experiments, total N=720.
limits: Human writers, Wikipedia events; not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Warns that an agent writing a failure story will make it look more inevitable the more causal detail it has. Treat the explanation as a hypothesis list, not a finding.
